{{Short description|Vector distance function}}
{{Distinguish|text=the pseudo-Euclidean metric of [[Minkowski spacetime]]}}
The '''Minkowski distance''' or '''Minkowski metric''' is a family of [[Metric (mathematics)|distance function]]s on a [[real coordinate space]], defined by taking the <math>p</math>th power along each coordinate, given a positive parameter <math>p</math>. That is, it is the distance function associated to a [[Lp_space#The_p-norm_in_finite_dimensions|p-norm]]. It is a generalization of both the [[Euclidean distance]] (<math>p=2</math>) and the [[Manhattan distance]] (<math>p=1</math>). It is named after the mathematician [[Hermann Minkowski]].
[[File:Minkowski_distance_examples.svg|thumb|Comparison of Chebyshev, Euclidean and taxicab/Manhattan distances for the hypotenuse of a 3-4-5 triangle on a chessboard (represented by a [[king (chess)|king]], an ant, and a [[wazir (chess)|wazir]]). The wazir moves like a [[rook (chess)|rook]] but only one square at a time.]]

== Definition ==

The Minkowski distance of order <math>p</math> (where <math>p\ge 1</math>) between two points
<math display="block">X = (x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n) \text{ and } Y = (y_1,y_2,\ldots,y_n) \in \R^n</math>
is defined as:
<math display="block">D_p\left(X,Y\right) = \biggl(\sum_{i=1}^n |x_i-y_i|^p\biggr)^{\frac{1}{p}}.</math> This is the metric associated to the [[norm (mathematics)|norm]] 
<math display="block">\|X\|_p = \left(\sum_{i=1}^n|x_i|^p\right)^{1/p}</math>

The Minkowski distance is a [[Metric (mathematics)|metric]] as a result of the [[Minkowski inequality]],<ref>{{citation
 | last = Şuhubi | first = Erdoğan S.
 | contribution = Chapter V: Metric Spaces
 | doi = 10.1007/978-94-017-0141-9_5
 | isbn = 9789401701419
 | pages = 261–356
 | publisher = Springer Netherlands
 | title = Functional Analysis
 | year = 2003}}</ref> 
<math display="block">\|X+Y\|_p\le \|X\|_p + \|Y\|_p.</math>
Geometrically, this is a norm because the [[unit ball]]s <math>\|X\|_p < 1</math> are bounded and open in the standard topology, contain the origin, and are [[convex set|convex]] and [[balanced set|balanced]] (invariant under <math>X\to -X</math>).

When <math>0 < p < 1,</math> the same formula does not define a metric because it fails to satisfy the [[triangle inequality]]. For example, distance between <math>(0, 0)</math> and <math>(1, 1)</math> is <math>2^{1/p} > 2,</math> but the point <math>(0, 1)</math> is at a distance <math>1</math> from both of these points. 

However, a metric can be obtained for these values by removing the exponent of <math>1/p</math>:
<math display="block">d_p(X,Y) = \sum_{i=1}^n |x_i-y_i|^p,\quad 0<p<1.</math>
The resulting metric is also an [[F-space|F-norm]], but does not come from a norm: the unit balls are not convex.

Minkowski distance is often used with <math>p = 1</math> or <math>p = 2</math>, which correspond to the [[Manhattan distance]] and the [[Euclidean distance]], respectively.<ref>{{citation
 | last1 = Zezula | first1 = Pavel
 | last2 = Amato | first2 = Giuseppe
 | last3 = Dohnal | first3 = Vlastislav
 | last4 = Batko | first4 = Michal
 | contribution = Chapter 1, Foundations of Metric Space Searching, Section 3.1, Minkowski Distances
 | doi = 10.1007/0-387-29151-2
 | isbn = 9780387291512
 | page = 10
 | publisher = Springer
 | series = Advances in Database Systems
 | title = Similarity Search: The Metric Space Approach
 | year = 2006}}</ref> In the limiting case of <math>p</math> approaching infinity, we obtain the [[Chebyshev distance]]:
<math display="block">\lim_{p \to \infty}{\biggl(\sum_{i=1}^n |x_i-y_i|^p\biggr)^\frac{1}{p}} = \max_{i=1}^n |x_i-y_i|.</math>

The limit as <math>p\to 0^+</math> of the metric <math>d_p</math> is sometimes called the [[Lp_space#When_p_=_0|0-distance]] or [[Hamming distance]]; it counts the number of coordinates <math>x_i</math> that differ from the coordinates <math>y_i</math>. This distance function is a metric, but like <math>d_p</math>, it does not arise from a norm.

The Minkowski distance can be viewed as a multiple of the [[power mean]] of the component-wise differences between <math>P</math> and <math>Q.</math>

The following figure shows unit circles (the [[level set]] of the distance function where all points are at the unit distance from the center) with various values of <math>p</math>:

== Applications ==
The Minkowski distance is useful in the field of [[machine learning]].<ref>{{Cite book |last=Duda |url=https://books.google.com/books/about/Pattern_Classification.html?id=NR-SzW2t7WYC |title=Pattern Classification |last2=Duda |first2=Richard O. |last3=Hart |first3=Peter E. |date=2006 |publisher=Wiley-India |isbn=978-81-265-1116-7 |language=en |p=31 }}</ref> Many popular machine learning algorithms use specific distance metrics such as the aforementioned to compare the similarity of two data points. Depending on the nature of the data being analyzed, various metrics can be used. The Minkowski metric is most useful for numerical datasets where one wants to determine the similarity of size between multiple datapoint vectors.
